route: A blind route: a formulation outside every approach family of the inventory. I replaced the probabilistic semantics of an SSG by a combinatorial one and then by a deterministic one: (a) ROUTINGS -- the value of a positional pair is the fraction of acyclic edge-selections that route the vertex to t1, a ratio of two integers with no arithmetic anywhere; (b) THE ROTOR GAME -- each average vertex carries a rotor that alternates between its two out-edges, chips are released one at a time from v0 and the two players route the chip at their own vertices, giving a finite DETERMINISTIC perfect-information game with no chance move whose value per chip is val(v0) up to an additive constant. Neither is a fixed-point theory, a polynomial class, a switching rule, an AUSO/readout question, a propagation calculus, a transport LP, a convex lift, an LCP/Lemke object, a homotopy, a query model, an order lattice, a variational identity, an oracle hierarchy, a realisation space or a random-facet bound; the chip game is not value iteration (it carries integer chip counts and a rotor state, and its players move chips, not numbers) and not the damping/bias/stopping-probability homotopies (nothing is deformed; the model is exact at every n).
object: The uniform counting measure on the ACYCLIC SELECTIONS ("routings") of the game digraph, together with its deterministic avatar, the rotor-router: a rotor configuration in {0,1}^Vavg, chips released one at a time from v0, and the two players routing the chip at their own vertices in the resulting finite deterministic perfect-information game ROT_rho(n).
headline: For every stopping SSG, every rotor configuration rho and every n, the n-chip rotor game -- a finite deterministic perfect-information game with no chance move -- has value M_rho(n) with |M_rho(n) - n*val(v0)| <= (1/2) sum_{u in Vavg} |val(u^0) - val(u^1)|, and the constant is attained.

results.name: The routing formula (elementary proof)
results.statement: Let (sigma,tau) be a positional pair of an SSG and call a map f from the non-sinks to {0,1} a SELECTION when it takes the strategy's index at every controlled vertex, and a ROUTING when its functional digraph v -> succ[v][f(v)] has no cycle. Write R(sigma,tau) for the set of routings. Then R(sigma,tau) is nonempty iff the chain M_{sigma,tau} is absorbing, and in that case val_{sigma,tau}(v) = |{f in R : the f-path from v ends at t1}| / |R(sigma,tau)| for every vertex v.
results.why_not_implied: thm:eval-stopfree evaluates val_{sigma,tau} as the solution of a linear programme with zero rows on the trap; it gives no cardinality, no set of combinatorial objects and no counting identity, and none follows from it in three lines.
results.argument: Nonemptiness: the attractor sweep A_0={t0,t1}, A_{k+1}=A_k u {v : some allowed successor in A_k}; if it exhausts the non-sinks, picking a successor of smaller rank gives an acyclic selection; otherwise the complement is closed for the chain (so the chain is not absorbing) and every selection maps it into itself, hence cycles. Formula: set c(v)=#{f in R : end_f(v)=t1}, c(t1)=|R|, c(t0)=0. At a controlled vertex c(v)=c(s) for the chosen successor s. At an average vertex u, split R by f(u) and, for a restriction f_{-u} with no cycle avoiding u, let d^i in {t0,t1,u} be the endpoint of the f_{-u}-path from u^(i). Then c(u)=A^0+A^1 with A^i=#{d^i=t1}, while c(u^(0))=A^0+#{d^0=t1,d^1!=u}+#{d^0=u,d^1=t1} and symmetrically; the four terms match term by term, so c(u^(0))+c(u^(1))=2c(u). Hence c/|R| solves (I-Q)x=b, which has a unique solution for an absorbing pair, and val_{sigma,tau} is a solution. NO IMPORT IS USED. HONESTY: the identity itself is NOT new to this project -- it is the 'forest balance' of a round-ten free-search route, confirmed then by the root agent on 800 and 4401 (game,pair) instances and deliberately kept OUT of frontier.tex because the only proof available went through the all-minors matrix-tree theorem, a fifth import. What is new is exactly the proof above, which removes that obstruction; from memory, unchecked, the identity is the absorbing case of the Markov-chain tree theorem (Kirchhoff, Tutte, Chaiken-Kleitman).
results.verification: Exact rational arithmetic throughout (fractions.Fraction). Brute-force enumeration of all 2^a selections against mycore.profile_value: 402 (game,pair) instances from 400 random games on 2-7 non-sinks, 0 violations; the nonemptiness characterisation checked against the chain-trap sweep on the same instances and on A0 (not stopping), 0 violations. On the paper's own families, every pair: G8 (N=8,a=5), S (7,4), S_r(4) (10,7), H_m(4) (12,9), G_m(5) (12,10), WD(2,2,4) (15,11), CC(2,3) (20,16) -- formula, determinant and nonemptiness all OK. Script verify_all.py sections 1-2.

results.name: The routing count is a common denominator, and equals a determinant
results.statement: With M the integer matrix on the non-sinks whose row at an average vertex u is 2e_u - e_{u^(0)} - e_{u^(1)} and at a controlled vertex v with chosen successor s is e_v - e_s (sink columns deleted), det M = |R(sigma,tau)|; hence the whole value vector of an absorbing pair is integral over the single integer |R(sigma,tau)| in [1,2^a]. This integer is NOT the det A_U of lem:denominator-sharp: det A_U divides |R| and is in general strictly smaller.
results.why_not_implied: lem:denominator-sharp bounds the denominator by det A_U <= 2^a via Hadamard and the watched-chain factorisation; it neither identifies any integer combinatorially nor states that the value vector is integral over a count of graph-theoretic objects, and the identification of det A_U with that count is in fact false.
results.argument: Induction on a using the linearity of the determinant in the row of one average vertex: that row is (e_u - e_{u^(0)}) + (e_u - e_{u^(1)}), so det M = det M^0 + det M^1 where M^i freezes u to index i, and |R| = |R^0| + |R^1|. Base case a=0: M = I-P with at most one 1 per row; acyclic gives a unitriangular matrix (det 1 = |R|), a cycle C gives |C| rows supported on the columns C forming I minus a cyclic permutation, so det 0 = |R|. The denominator statement is then the routing formula.
results.verification: det M compared with the brute-force count on the same 402 pairs and on all the named families above: 0 mismatches. Divisibility of every value's denominator by det M checked on the paper's LARGE published games without enumeration -- B2_small_GAME.json (N=138, a=130, 64 pairs), H11_m5_GAME.json (N=260, a=253, 32 pairs), B1_game.json (N=58, a=53, 8 pairs): 0 violations; log2|R| there is about 127, 247, 51. det A_U recomputed from the proof of lem:denominator-sharp (detAU.py) on 253 pairs: it divides |R| in 253/253 and equals it in 192/253. Script verify_all.py sections 1-3 and 9.

results.name: The rotor sandwich
results.statement: Let G be stopping, w = val, A(G) = sum_{u in Vavg} |w(u^0) - w(u^1)| <= a. In the n-chip rotor game ROT_rho(n) -- chips released one at a time from v0, average vertices alternating their two out-edges, Max and Min routing the chip at their own vertices, payoff the number of chips stopping at t1 -- the value M_rho(n) exists and satisfies |M_rho(n) - n*val(v0)| <= A(G)/2 for every n >= 1 and every rotor configuration rho. Hence val(v0) = lim_n M_rho(n)/n for every rho.
results.why_not_implied: thm:energy is the identity sum_v N_v Delta_v^2 = 4w(1-w) for the expected visit counts of the stochastic game; it is an L^2 identity about the chain, says nothing about a deterministic process, and gives no bound on any deterministic game's value. thm:contraction's rate 1-2^{-a} governs value iteration on real vectors, not a chip count.
results.argument: Termination: an infinite play would make the set U of infinitely visited vertices a trap (an average vertex visited infinitely often sends the chip both ways because its rotor alternates, so both its successors are in U), contradicting lem:trapchar. Identity: telescoping any h with h(t0)=0, h(t1)=1 and 2h(u)=h(u^0)+h(u^1) along the chips' paths gives OUT_n = n h(v0) + sum_{u in Vavg} s_u [K_u odd] delta_u + sum over controlled visits of (h(chosen) - h(v)), with delta_u = (h(u^0)-h(u^1))/2 and s_u = +-1 from the rotor start, because the j-th visit to u contributes (-1)^{j-1} s_u delta_u and consecutive visits cancel in pairs. Take h = val: Max routing to an optimal successor kills his terms, Min's terms are >= 0, and the average terms are >= -A/2; dually for Min. The rotor deviation is bounded INDEPENDENTLY of n -- that is the whole content.
results.verification: The exact identity checked on 672 runs (200 random stopping games, all pairs, 3 random rotor starts, n in 1..12) in exact rational arithmetic: 0 failures. The sandwich checked against the exact game value M_rho(n), computed by backward induction on the state (chips left, position, rotor configuration) in chipgame.py, on E1 for n <= 10 and all three rotor starts. Script verify_all.py sections 4-5.

results.name: Exactness over a rotor period
results.statement: Fix an absorbing pair and let Phi send a rotor configuration to the one left by one chip released at v0. If rho is a recurrent point of Phi with period p (p <= 2^a), then releasing p chips from rho returns the rotor configuration, every average vertex is visited an even number of times, and val_{sigma,tau}(v0) = OUT_p / p exactly. The value of a positional pair is therefore computed by a deterministic process whose only arithmetic is counting, and its denominator divides p.
results.why_not_implied: thm:eval-stopfree evaluates a pair by solving a linear programme in rational arithmetic; it contains no deterministic combinatorial process, no period, and no statement that the value is a ratio of two integers produced by such a process.
results.argument: Phi is well defined because the walk terminates; every orbit of a self-map of a finite set is eventually periodic; the rotor at u has period two, so Phi^p rho = rho forces every visit count even, and then the deviation term and the controlled term of the rotor identity both vanish.
results.verification: 224 (game, pair, rotor start) instances from 200 random stopping games: OUT_p/p equals val_{sigma,tau}(v0) exactly in all of them, and the period p divides |R(sigma,tau)| in 224/224 (and, over a larger sweep of 884 instances, in 884/884; p equals the denominator of val(v0) in 999 of 1401 instances, so p is a proper multiple of the denominator in general). On the paper's instances: S (period 2 and 4), H_m(3) (period 16, OUT=9, val=9/16). Script verify_all.py section 4.

results.name: The derandomisation is lossy, the constant is attained, and positional play is not optimal in the rotor game
results.statement: For the stopping SSG E1 on five vertices (Vmax={v0}, Vavg={u1,u2}, v0->(u1,u2), u1->(t1,t0), u2->(t1,t0)) one has val(v0)=1/2, A(E1)=2 and, for the rotor start rho=(0,0) and every even n, M_rho(n) = n/2 + 1 = n val(v0) + A(E1)/2, so the sandwich is tight; while the best Max can force with a POSITIONAL strategy is ceil(n/2). Hence positional strategies are not optimal in the rotor game from n=2 on, and no choice of n makes the rotor game's value equal n val(v0).
results.why_not_implied: thm:determinacy is positional determinacy of the SSG itself; the rotor game is a different game whose state carries the rotor configuration and the chip budget, and nothing about its optimal strategies follows from positional determinacy of the SSG in three lines.
results.argument: Upper bound from the sandwich. Lower bound by the explicit adaptive Max strategy 'send each chip to a vertex whose rotor points at t1 if there is one, else to u1': the first two chips win and leave both rotors at 1, after which the chips alternate t0,t1,..., giving OUT_n = 2 + floor((n-2)/2). A positional Max uses one u_i only, whose rotor alternates from 0, giving ceil(n/2).
results.verification: Exact game solve (chipgame.py, backward induction over (chips left, position, rotor configuration)) on the game built from E1_GAME.json: M(n) = 2,3,4,5,6 for n = 2,4,6,8,10 against n*val + A/2 = 2,3,4,5,6 and best positional 1,2,3,4,5; val(v0)=1/2 recomputed from the game by brute-force max-min over all pairs. Script verify_all.py section 5.

results.name: The rotor game needs exponentially many chips
results.statement: For m >= 1 let RC(m) be the stopping SSG on N = m+17 vertices: a complete binary tree of seven Max vertices with root v0 and eight average leaves u_1..u_8, each u_i -> (q_1,t0), above an average chain q_i -> (t1,q_{i+1}) (i<m), q_m -> (t1,t0). Then val(v0) = val(u_i) = 1/2 - 2^{-(m+1)} < 1/2, yet for the rotor start rho == 0 one has M_rho(n) > n/2 for every n < 7(2^m - 1) = 2^{Omega(N)}. Deciding the bit of prob:main from M_rho(n) therefore needs 2^{Omega(N)} chips.
results.why_not_implied: thm:vi-lower says the Shapley iteration on real vectors needs exponentially many rounds on a player-free family; it says nothing about the number of chips of a deterministic chip game, whose error term is not a contraction residue but the fixed constant A(G)/2, and whose lower bound here comes from Max's ability to time the rotors, a phenomenon absent from value iteration.
results.argument: With rho == 0 every delta_u of the rotor identity is positive (delta_{u_i} = val(q_1)/2, delta_{q_i} = (1 - val(q_{i+1}))/2) and every Max increment vanishes because all successors inside the tree have equal value; so OUT_n >= n val(v0) under any Max play, and for n <= 7 the schedule 'i-th chip to u_i' gives OUT_n = n. For n >= 7 that schedule followed by 'all later chips to u_8' leaves K_{u_1} = ... = K_{u_7} = 1 odd, so OUT_n >= n val(v0) + (7/2) val(q_1) = n/2 - n 2^{-(m+1)} + (7/2)(1 - 2^{-m}), which exceeds n/2 exactly when n < 7(2^m - 1). Finally M_rho(n) >= OUT_n since RC(m) has no Min vertex.
results.verification: The games are built and everything is measured FROM THE GAME. is_stopping true for m = 3,4,5; brute-force max-min value equals 1/2 - 2^{-(m+1)} for m = 3,4,5 (7/16, 15/32, 31/64); A/2 = 35/8, 75/16, 155/32. The rotor process is simulated on the game in exact arithmetic for m = 4,6,8,10 up to n = 8*2^m: 2*OUT_n > n holds for every n <= 7(2^m - 1) in all four, the first failure occurring at n = 120, 504, 2040, 8184 (i.e. 8*2^m - 8, so the proved bound is conservative), and the minimum excess OUT_n - n*val over n >= 7 is exactly (7/2)val(q_1) = 105/32, 441/128, 1785/512, 7161/2048, matching the bound with equality. Script verify_all.py section 6; games RC_m4/m8/m12_GAME.json.

results.name: The behavioural value is a ratio of multilinear forms, and the retyping identity
results.statement: Weight a selection f by omega_p(f) = prod_{v in C} p_v^{[f(v)=1]} (1-p_v)^{[f(v)=0]} and let B(p) be the total weight of the routings and A(p) that of the routings sending v0 to t1. Then A and B are multilinear in p, B > 0 on [0,1]^C for a stopping game, and A(p)/B(p) is the value at v0 when each controlled vertex v takes its index 1 with probability p_v. Consequently the value is a Moebius function of each single p_v, hence monotone in it; and at p_v = 1/2 -- retyping v as an average vertex -- the value vector is exactly the routing-count-weighted convex combination (Z^0 v^0 + Z^1 v^1)/(Z^0 + Z^1) of the two frozen value vectors.
results.why_not_implied: thm:profile-uso orients the 2^{|C|} CORNERS of the profile cube and identifies the orientation with a P-matrix LCP's; it provides no interpolation over the interior of the cube, no functional form for it, and in particular no formula for the value at the centre in terms of counts.
results.argument: Each routing contributes a monomial of degree at most one in each p_v, so A and B are multilinear; freezing the controlled coordinates recovers the routing formula, and for general p the same term-by-term proof applies to the chain in which v has out-edge probabilities 1-p_v, p_v. B(p) > 0 because B is a convex combination of the corner counts |R(sigma,tau)| >= 1. Monotonicity is that of a ratio of two affine functions with a nonvanishing denominator; the retyping identity is the corner expansion at p_v = 1/2.
results.verification: A(p)/B(p) computed by brute-force enumeration of the weighted routings and compared with the value of the biased chain solved exactly: 90 (game, p) instances with p on the grid of sixths, 0 mismatches. The retyping identity checked at every vertex on 90 random stopping games with a random controlled vertex retyped and the other controlled vertices randomly frozen: 0 mismatches. Script verify_all.py sections 7-8.

results.name: Bounded routing count collapses into the few-denominator class
results.statement: Put nu(G) = max over absorbing pairs of |R(sigma,tau)| <= 2^a. Every value of every pair, hence every letter of the value alphabet, has denominator dividing nu(G); so for every polynomial q the class {G stopping : nu(G) <= q(N)} is contained in the class of thm:few-denominator and is solved in O(N^2 nu(G)^2) by the rounded iteration of thm:alphabet-iteration. In particular |R| = 2^a for every pair iff the game digraph is acyclic, in which case the routing measure is the uniform product measure. No polynomial class outside the eight known ones arises from a bound on the number of routings.
results.why_not_implied: thm:few-denominator is a statement about games with a small common denominator; it does not mention routings, does not say that a graph-theoretic count bounds the denominator, and the containment therefore has to be proved, not read off.
results.argument: Immediate from the routing formula and cor:fresh19-den, plus the fact that thm:alphabet-iteration needs no advance knowledge of the denominator. The product case is the observation that a cycle of the digraph is contained in some selection, and a selection containing a cycle is not a routing.
results.verification: No new measurement is needed beyond the routing formula's; the containment is a two-line consequence. Reported as a COLLAPSE (rule C of the round): the routing view yields no new polynomial class.

restatements.label: lem:denominator-sharp
restatements.note: |R(sigma,tau)| <= 2^a re-derives the 2^a denominator bound, but weakly: det A_U divides |R| and is often strictly smaller (192 of 253 pairs equal), so the paper's bound stays the sharper one.

restatements.label: thm:determinacy
restatements.note: clause (1) of the multilinear-fraction proposition -- randomising at a controlled vertex never beats both pure choices -- is positional determinacy for behavioural strategies; the proof through routings is new but the statement is not.

restatements.label: thm:avg-acyclic
restatements.note: the product case of the routing measure (|R| = 2^a for every pair, i.e. an acyclic game digraph) is the setting in which thm:avg-acyclic already gives tractability; nothing new follows from the counting picture there.

restatements.label: thm:few-avg
restatements.note: the exact rotor evaluation val_{sigma,tau}(v0) = OUT_p/p costs p <= 2^a chips of poly(N) steps each, so as an algorithm for a fixed pair it lands inside the poly(N)2^a regime of thm:few-avg.

gap: GAP: for every absorbing pair (sigma,tau) of a stopping SSG and every recurrent rotor configuration rho, the period of the map Phi (release one chip at v0) DIVIDES the number of routings |R(sigma,tau)|. (Measured true in 884 of 884 (game, pair, rotor start) instances, and in the 224 instances of the main sweep; proved here only that the denominator of val_{sigma,tau}(v0) divides the period and that the period is at most 2^a. From memory and unchecked against any source, this is the rotor-router group / abelian sandpile statement that the group order equals the number of spanning forests.)
next_steps: (1) Integrate thm:fresh19-routing and cor:fresh19-den: they supply exactly what kept round ten's forest balance out of frontier.tex -- a first-principles proof needing no fifth import -- and they correct that route's false identification of det A_U with the routing count. (2) Settle the gap (period divides |R|); it would make the rotor period an exact combinatorial invariant sitting between the denominator and 2^a. (3) The routing view turns 'val(v0) >= 1/2' into 'the losing routings inject into the winning ones', a certificate format the paper does not have (def:bracket is the closest); the sharp question it raises is whether a polynomially describable injection always exists for a one-player game -- a proof-complexity question about prob:main, not a rule. (4) The rotor game is a deterministic game whose value determines val; the honest cost is its state space (chips, position, rotor), and thm:fresh19-chips shows the chip budget alone must be exponential, so any gain must come from structure in the rotor dynamics, not from more chips. (5) Not pursued for want of time: whether the improvement orientation of the Max cube, which in this language is the sign pattern of the gradient of a ratio of two multilinear forms with nonnegative integer coefficients, is constrained by that form -- a possible new realisability obstruction to set beside Holt-Klee.

I have not seen a rotor derandomisation of a GAME (two players routing chips at their own vertices) anywhere, and no such object exists in this project; the sandwich, its attainment, and the chip lower bound are, to the best of my knowledge, new.

\subsection{Routings: the value as a ratio of counts}\label{sec:fresh19}

Throughout this subsection $G$ is an SSG, $S$ its set of non-sinks, $a=|\Vavg|$,
and $(\sigma,\tau)$ a positional pair.  Nothing below uses the Shapley operator,
a linear programme, a cube of strategies or a propagation calculus: the value is
read off a finite set of combinatorial objects by counting.

\begin{definition}[Selections and routings]\label{fresh19:def-routing}
A \emph{selection} for $(\sigma,\tau)$ is a map $f\colon S\to\{0,1\}$ with
$f(v)=i$ at $v\in\Vmax$ when $\sigma(v)=v^{(i)}$ and $f(v)=i$ at $v\in\Vmin$
when $\tau(v)=v^{(i)}$; at $v\in\Vavg$ the value $f(v)$ is free.  (Selections
are maps to \emph{indices}, so a vertex whose two out-edges coincide still has
two selections through it.)  The \emph{functional digraph} of $f$ sends $v\in S$
to $v^{(f(v))}$.  A selection is a \emph{routing} if its functional digraph has
no cycle, equivalently if from every vertex the $f$-path reaches a sink; the
$f$-path from $v$ then has a well-defined endpoint
$\mathrm{end}_f(v)\in\{t_0,t_1\}$.  Write $\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)$ for the set
of routings; there are exactly $2^{a}$ selections, so
$|\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)|\le2^{a}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[When routings exist]\label{fresh19:lem-nonempty}
$\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)\ne\emptyset$ if and only if the Markov chain
$M_{\sigma,\tau}$ is absorbing.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Call $w$ an \emph{allowed successor} of $v\in S$ if $w=v^{(i)}$ for some index
$i$ permitted to $f$ at $v$.  Let $A_0=\{t_0,t_1\}$ and
$A_{k+1}=A_k\cup\{v:\text{some allowed successor of }v\text{ lies in }A_k\}$, and
$A_\infty=\bigcup_kA_k$.  If $A_\infty\supseteq S$, choosing at each $v$ an
allowed successor of strictly smaller rank gives a selection with no cycle.  If
$U:=S\setminus A_\infty\ne\emptyset$, every allowed successor of a vertex of $U$
lies in $U$, so $U$ is closed for $M_{\sigma,\tau}$ and no vertex of $U$ ever
reaches a sink; and every selection maps the finite nonempty set $U$ into
itself, hence has a cycle.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The routing formula]\label{fresh19:thm-routing}
Let $(\sigma,\tau)$ be an absorbing pair, $Z:=|\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)|\ge1$ and
$c(v):=|\{f\in\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau):\mathrm{end}_f(v)=t_1\}|$ for $v\in S$.
Then $v_{\sigma,\tau}(v)=c(v)/Z$ for every $v\in S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $c(t_1):=Z$, $c(t_0):=0$, $x:=c/Z$.  At a controlled vertex $v$ with chosen
successor $s$, $\mathrm{end}_f(v)=\mathrm{end}_f(s)$ for every routing, so
$x(v)=x(s)$.  Let $u\in\Vavg$ and split
$\mathcal R=\mathcal R^0\sqcup\mathcal R^1$ by $f(u)$.  Write $f_{-u}$ for the
restriction of a selection to $S\setminus\{u\}$ and let $P$ be the set of those
$f_{-u}$ with no cycle avoiding $u$.  For $f_{-u}\in P$ the $f_{-u}$-path from
$u^{(i)}$ cannot cycle, so it ends at $t_0$, $t_1$ or $u$; call that endpoint
$d^{i}\in\{t_0,t_1,u\}$, so $\mathcal R^{i}=\{f_{-u}\in P:d^{i}\ne u\}$.  With
$A^{i}:=|\{f_{-u}\in P:d^{i}=t_1\}|$ we get $c(u)=A^{0}+A^{1}$ and
\[
  c(u^{(0)})=A^{0}+|\{d^{0}=t_1,d^{1}\ne u\}|+|\{d^{0}=u,d^{1}=t_1\}|,
\]
the first summand counting the $f\in\mathcal R^{0}$ and the others the
$f\in\mathcal R^{1}$; symmetrically for $c(u^{(1)})$.  Since
$A^{0}=|\{d^{0}=t_1,d^{1}\ne u\}|+|\{d^{0}=t_1,d^{1}=u\}|$ and likewise for
$A^{1}$, adding gives $c(u^{(0)})+c(u^{(1)})=2c(u)$.  Hence $x$ solves
$(I-Q)x_{|S}=b$ for the substochastic matrix $Q$ of $M_{\sigma,\tau}$; for an
absorbing pair $\rho(Q)<1$, the solution is unique, and $v_{\sigma,\tau}$ is one.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The routing count is a common denominator]\label{fresh19:cor-den}
Let $M$ be the integer matrix indexed by $S$ whose row at $u\in\Vavg$ is
$2e_u-e_{u^{(0)}}-e_{u^{(1)}}$ and whose row at a controlled $v$ with chosen
successor $s$ is $e_v-e_s$ (sink columns deleted).  Then
$\det M=|\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)|$, and the whole value vector of the pair is
integral over that one number, which lies in $[1,2^{a}]$.  It is \emph{not} the
integer $\det A_U$ of \Cref{lem:denominator-sharp}, which divides it and is in
general strictly smaller (equality in $192$ of $253$ pairs measured).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $a$.  For $a=0$, $M=I-P$ with at most one $1$ per row: if the
functional digraph is acyclic a topological order makes $M$ unitriangular, so
$\det M=1=|\mathcal R|$; if it has a cycle $C$, the rows of $C$ vanish outside
the columns $C$ and there form $I$ minus a cyclic permutation, so
$\det M=0=|\mathcal R|$.  For $a\ge1$ pick $u\in\Vavg$ and write its row as
$(e_u-e_{u^{(0)}})+(e_u-e_{u^{(1)}})$; the determinant is linear in that row, so
$\det M=\det M^{0}+\det M^{1}$ with $M^{i}$ the matrix with $u$ frozen to index
$i$, and $|\mathcal R|=|\mathcal R^{0}|+|\mathcal R^{1}|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Attribution]\label{fresh19:rem-attr}
The identity of \Cref{fresh19:thm-routing} is the \emph{forest balance} of a
round-ten free-search route, confirmed then by the root agent on $800$ and on
$4401$ (game, pair) instances and deliberately kept out of this paper because
the only proof available went through the all-minors matrix-tree theorem, which
would be a fifth import.  What is new above is the proof --- a term-by-term
count and the linearity of a determinant in one row --- so the identity can now
be stated without any import; and that route's downstream claim that $\det A_U$
\emph{is} the routing count was refuted then and is corrected in
\Cref{fresh19:cor-den}.  From memory and unchecked against any source, the
identity is the absorbing case of the Markov-chain tree theorem (Kirchhoff,
Tutte, Chaiken--Kleitman), and the rotor facts below are in the neighbourhood of
the rotor-router literature (Priezzhev--Dhar, Holroyd--Propp) --- but the game
with two players is not.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[The product case]\label{fresh19:cor-acyclic}
$|\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)|=2^{a}$ iff the digraph in which average vertices keep
both out-edges and controlled vertices keep the chosen one is acyclic; then the
routing measure is the uniform product measure on $\{0,1\}^{\Vavg}$.  This holds
for every pair simultaneously iff the game digraph is acyclic.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If the digraph is acyclic so is every selection; a cycle uses at most one
out-edge at each of its vertices, so some selection (and some pair) contains it.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The routing count is a few-denominator parameter]\label{fresh19:prop-collapse}
Put $\nu(G):=\max_{(\sigma,\tau)}|\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)|\le2^{a}$ over
absorbing pairs.  Every value of every pair, hence every letter of $\Lambda(G)$,
has denominator dividing $\nu(G)$; so for every polynomial $q$ the class
$\{G\ \text{stopping}:\nu(G)\le q(N)\}$ lies inside the class of
\Cref{thm:few-denominator} and is solved in $O(N^{2}\nu(G)^{2})$ by
\Cref{thm:alphabet-iteration}.  No polynomial class outside the eight known ones
arises from a bound on the number of routings.
\end{proposition}

\subsection{The rotor game: the same value without probability}

\begin{definition}[The $n$-chip rotor game]\label{fresh19:def-rotor}
A \emph{rotor configuration} is $\rho\in\{0,1\}^{\Vavg}$.  A chip at a sink
stops; at a controlled vertex its owner moves it to a successor of his choice;
at $u\in\Vavg$ it moves to $u^{(\rho_u)}$ and then $\rho_u$ is replaced by
$1-\rho_u$.  In $\mathrm{ROT}_\rho(n)$ the chips $1,\dots,n$ are released one at
a time from $v_0$, the next only after the previous has stopped, the rotor
configuration persisting; Max maximises and Min minimises the number
$\mathrm{OUT}_n$ of chips stopping at $t_1$.  Both players see the whole state.
Its value is $M_\rho(n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Termination]\label{fresh19:lem-terminate}
On a stopping SSG every play of $\mathrm{ROT}_\rho(n)$ is finite; under
positional play one chip is absorbed within $N2^{a}$ steps.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If a chip walked for ever, the set $U$ of vertices visited infinitely often
would satisfy: every vertex of $U$ has a successor in $U$; an average vertex of
$U$ is entered infinitely often, so its rotor alternates and both successors lie
in $U$; and $U$ contains no sink.  So $U$ is a trap, contradicting
\Cref{lem:trapchar}.  Under positional play (position, rotor configuration)
determines its successor, and there are $N2^{a}$ such pairs.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The rotor identity]\label{fresh19:thm-identity}
Let $h\colon V\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $h(t_0)=0$, $h(t_1)=1$ and
$2h(u)=h(u^{(0)})+h(u^{(1)})$ at every $u\in\Vavg$.  Run $\mathrm{ROT}_\rho(n)$
under any play, let $K_u$ be the number of visits to $u\in\Vavg$, put
$s_u:=+1$ if $\rho_u=0$ and $-1$ otherwise, and
$\delta_u:=\tfrac12(h(u^{(0)})-h(u^{(1)}))$.  Then
\[
  \mathrm{OUT}_n=n\,h(v_0)+\sum_{u\in\Vavg}s_u[K_u\ \text{odd}]\,\delta_u
   +\sum_{v\in C}\ \sum_{\text{visits to }v}\bigl(h(\text{chosen successor})-h(v)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Telescope $h$ along each chip's path and sum the increments by vertex; the
$j$-th visit to $u\in\Vavg$ contributes $(-1)^{j-1}s_u\delta_u$, and consecutive
visits cancel in pairs.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The rotor sandwich]\label{fresh19:cor-sandwich}
Let $G$ be stopping, $w=\val$ and
$A(G):=\sum_{u\in\Vavg}|w(u^{(0)})-w(u^{(1)})|\le a$.  Then for every $n\ge1$
and every $\rho$,
\[
   \bigl|M_\rho(n)-n\,\val(v_0)\bigr|\;\le\;\tfrac12A(G),
\]
so $\val(v_0)=\lim_n M_\rho(n)/n$ for every $\rho$: the value of an SSG is the
growth rate of a deterministic perfect-information game with no chance moves.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take $h=w$ in \Cref{fresh19:thm-identity}.  Max routing every chip to an optimal
successor kills his terms, Min's terms are $\ge0$, and the average terms are at
least $-\tfrac12A(G)$; dually for Min.  The game is finite by
\Cref{fresh19:lem-terminate}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exactness over a rotor period]\label{fresh19:thm-period}
Fix an absorbing pair and let $\Phi$ send $\rho$ to the rotor configuration left
by one chip released at $v_0$.  If $\rho$ is recurrent for $\Phi$ with period
$p\le2^{a}$, then every $K_u$ over those $p$ chips is even and
$v_{\sigma,\tau}(v_0)=\mathrm{OUT}_p/p$ exactly; in particular the denominator
of $v_{\sigma,\tau}(v_0)$ divides $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Phi$ is well defined by \Cref{fresh19:lem-terminate} and every orbit is
eventually periodic; the rotor at $u$ has period two, so $\Phi^{p}\rho=\rho$
forces $K_u$ even.  Apply \Cref{fresh19:thm-identity} with
$h=v_{\sigma,\tau}$: the controlled increments vanish and every average term
carries $[K_u\ \text{odd}]=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The derandomisation is lossy, and the constant is attained]\label{fresh19:prop-lossy}
Let $E_1$ be the stopping SSG on five vertices with $\Vmax=\{v_0\}$,
$\Vavg=\{u_1,u_2\}$, $v_0\to(u_1,u_2)$, $u_1\to(t_1,t_0)$, $u_2\to(t_1,t_0)$.
Then $\val(v_0)=\tfrac12$, $A(E_1)=2$, and for $\rho=(0,0)$ and every even $n$,
$M_\rho(n)=\tfrac n2+1=n\val(v_0)+\tfrac12A(E_1)$, so
\Cref{fresh19:cor-sandwich} is tight; while the best Max can force
\emph{positionally} is $\lceil n/2\rceil$, so positional play is strictly
suboptimal in the rotor game from $n=2$ on.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound is \Cref{fresh19:cor-sandwich}.  For the lower bound Max sends
each chip to a vertex whose rotor points at $t_1$ if there is one and to $u_1$
otherwise: the first two chips reach $t_1$ and leave both rotors at $1$, after
which the chips alternate $t_0,t_1,\dots$, giving
$\mathrm{OUT}_n=2+\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor$.  A positional Max uses one $u_i$ only,
whose rotor alternates from $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The rotor game needs exponentially many chips]\label{fresh19:thm-chips}
For $m\ge1$ let $\mathrm{RC}(m)$ be the stopping SSG on $N=m+17$ vertices: a
complete binary tree of seven Max vertices with root $v_0$ and leaves
$u_1,\dots,u_8\in\Vavg$, each $u_i\to(q_1,t_0)$, above a chain
$q_1,\dots,q_m\in\Vavg$ with $q_i\to(t_1,q_{i+1})$ for $i<m$ and
$q_m\to(t_1,t_0)$.  Then $\val(q_i)=1-2^{-(m-i+1)}$ and
$\val(v_0)=\val(u_i)=\tfrac12-2^{-(m+1)}<\tfrac12$, while for $\rho\equiv0$
\[
   M_\rho(n)>\tfrac n2\qquad\text{for every }n<7(2^{m}-1)=2^{\Omega(N)} .
\]
Deciding the bit of \Cref{prob:main} from $M_\rho(n)$ needs $2^{\Omega(N)}$ chips.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every average vertex has a sink among its successors, so no average vertex lies
in a trap and no set of tree vertices alone is one: $G$ is stopping.  With
$\rho\equiv0$ every $\delta_u$ is positive ($\delta_{u_i}=\tfrac12\val(q_1)$,
$\delta_{q_i}=\tfrac12(1-\val(q_{i+1}))$ with $q_{m+1}:=t_0$) and $s_u=+1$; all
Max increments vanish because every tree vertex has two successors of equal
value.  So $\mathrm{OUT}_n\ge n\val(v_0)$ under any play, and for $n\le7$ the
schedule sending the $i$-th chip to $u_i$ gives $\mathrm{OUT}_n=n$.  For $n\ge7$
that schedule, followed by sending every later chip to $u_8$, leaves
$K_{u_1}=\dots=K_{u_7}=1$ odd, so
$\mathrm{OUT}_n\ge n\val(v_0)+\tfrac72\val(q_1)
=\tfrac n2-n2^{-(m+1)}+\tfrac72(1-2^{-m})$, which exceeds $n/2$ exactly when
$n<7(2^{m}-1)$.  Finally $M_\rho(n)\ge\mathrm{OUT}_n$, there being no Min vertex.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Biased routings}

\begin{proposition}[The behavioural value is a ratio of multilinear forms]\label{fresh19:prop-mixed}
For $p\in[0,1]^{C}$ weight a selection by
$\omega_p(f)=\prod_{v\in C}p_v^{[f(v)=1]}(1-p_v)^{[f(v)=0]}$ and let $B(p)$ be
the total weight of the acyclic selections (all coordinates free) and $A(p)$
that of those with $\mathrm{end}_f(v_0)=t_1$.  Then $A,B$ are multilinear,
$B>0$ on $[0,1]^{C}$ for a stopping game, and $A(p)/B(p)$ is the value at $v_0$
of the chain in which each $v\in C$ takes index~$1$ with probability $p_v$.
Consequently (1) in each coordinate the value is a M\"obius function of $p_v$,
hence monotone --- randomising at a controlled vertex never beats both pure
choices; and (2) at $p_v=\tfrac12$, i.e.\ retyping $v$ as an average vertex, the
value vector is $\bigl(Z^{0}v^{0}+Z^{1}v^{1}\bigr)/(Z^{0}+Z^{1})$, the two
frozen value vectors weighted by the numbers $Z^{i}$ of routings with $f(v)=i$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each selection contributes a monomial of degree at most one in each $p_v$.
Freezing $C$ to a corner recovers \Cref{fresh19:thm-routing}, and for general
$p$ the same term-by-term proof applies to the chain with out-edge
probabilities $1-p_v,p_v$ at $v$.  $B(p)>0$ because $B$ is a convex combination
of the corner counts $|\mathcal R(\sigma,\tau)|\ge1$.  (1) is the monotonicity
of a ratio of affine functions with nonvanishing denominator; (2) is the corner
expansion at $p_v=\tfrac12$.
\end{proof}
